#6566. The 20 Most Iconic Colognes of All Time, According to GQ in 2026

The first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece. Well, as a longtime fragrance editor, I get a similar feeling when I smell Guerlain’s iconic Vétiver scent (or, more recently, Penhaligon’s Halfeti). These fragrances smelled exceptional when they debuted, still do today, probably still will a hundred years from now. And while fragrance, like any art form, has its trends, the truly great scents (and songs) have a way of deflecting them and singing on.

All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years. To do so, I dug through the history of men’s fragrance to put together a list of some of the most iconic colognes of all time. Scents that defined an era, changed the course of perfumery, or smelled so good that folks never stopped wearing them.

Our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time. You might love some more than others, but all have earned their place in the fragrance pantheon. Here are 20 of the most popular, influential, and enduring colognes ever made, and exactly why they’ve lasted.

Is there a more classic cologne than Acqua di Parma’s Colonia? Launched in 1916, this timeless citrus is the original Italian splash, and it would be criminal not to include it on a list of this caliber. That crisp, bright citrus opening is unmistakable, but there’s so much more going on beneath the surface as it dries down, with the supporting notes weaving in and out without ever stealing the show. Herbaceous hints of lavender and rosemary add herbal hues, while earthy vetiver and patchouli mingle with the smooth warmth of sandalwood as it settles on the skin. This is one of the great daily drivers, if not the very archetype of what an everyday cologne could or should be. It’s a 10/10 blend of citrus, aromatics, and woods, and more than a century on, still smells as sophisticated as ever.

I’ve written about Guerlain Vétiver so many times, you’d think I’d have run out of ways to sing its praises. But I could go forever. Few fragrances have done more to establish vetiver as a leading note, and since its 1959 debut, this masterpiece has remained every bit as relevant and wearable. It beautifully captures vetiver’s fresher, greener side, rather than leaning into its smoky, earthy character. There’s a crispness, with bright citrus, a touch of spice, and grassy vetiver balanced by subtle tobacco and woods, like the first cool, earthy dew on a spring morning. Elegant and confident, it oozes the kind of sophistication I imagine old-school Hollywood leading men appreciating, yet it wears just as well today, whether you're suited up or simply going about your day.

Ask me to name the most influential luxury fragrance of the 21st century, and there’s a good chance I’d say Aventus (notice, I said “luxury”). I’ve seen firsthand just how many guys made their first foray into high-end fragrance with this icon, and while I now often gravitate toward some of the deeper cuts in Creed’s storied catalog, every time I wear Aventus, the compliments roll in. Since its 2010 debut, it has inspired countless imitators and the inevitable fragrance fatigue that comes with being a phenomenon, yet I don’t think it’s lost an ounce of its appeal. To me, it's the ultimate wedding fragrance, a perfect blend of bright citrus and pineapple, aromatic freshness, and rich, smoky woods that’s refined without being fussy. The defining fragrance of the 2010s? I’d make that argument any day. Aventus will always have a place on my shelf.

No. 89 is one of the great British gentlemen’s fragrances, and few colognes capture Bond-like elegance quite like it. And it tracks: Introduced in 1951, No. 89 counted James Bond creator Ian Fleming among its famous admirers, while Cary Grant and Sir Alec Guinness were reportedly devotees as well. The scent itself is traditional in the best way, a classically composed fougère with crisp, almost barbershop-like citrus and lavender freshness, subtle florals, warming spice, and a smooth, woody base of vetiver and oakmoss. Aromatic, gently spicy, and impeccably polished, it’s the olfactory equivalent of a beautifully tailored Savile Row suit. More than seven decades on, No. 89 is proof that class and character never go out of style.

Back in the ’90s, CK One was everywhere. From Wall Street execs to flannel-wearing creatives; its intoxicating freshness just captured the zeitgeist. It was also one of the first mainstream fragrances marketed as unisex. (Almost an afterthought for fragrance fans today, it was a fairly novel concept then.) And while countless fragrances have followed in its footsteps, this citrusy, green, woodsy, lightly sweet profile still more than holds up. A surprising amount is going on here, too: a bright medley of citrus and tropical fruits, a floral heart with hints of spice, and a clean, musky base of cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s an icon that helped define a generation, and it works just as well day or night, on pretty much anyone. And perhaps most impressively, after all these years, CK One still smells unmistakably like CK One.

Much like his clothing, Ralph Lauren’s original Polo fragrance has left an indelible mark on American style. Launched in 1978, the unmistakable green-bottled cologne helped define what a classic masculine fragrance could smell like: sophisticated, confident, and unapologetically aromatic. And while nearly five decades have passed, there’s still nothing quite like it. That signature pine-heavy character is front and center, surrounded by a rich blend of herb and spices with bergamot adding brightness and leather lending rugged, earthy depth. It’s bold, woody, green, and distinctly old-school, but that’s precisely its charm. It’s undergone reformulations over the years, and its assertive character won’t appeal to everyone, but there’s no denying its place in the fragrance hall of fame. Some colognes come and go, but Polo isn’t going anywhere.

When I spotted that frosted bottle in my dad’s medicine cabinet and wore it for the first time, I had no idea that this scent would spark a lifelong fragrance obsession. Armani’s 1996 icon, Acqua di Giò, has been worn by millions, referenced endlessly, and spawned countless flankers, but the original remains one of those rare mass-appeal designer colognes that have stood the test of time. Why? Because it’s just so wearable. Long before the niche fragrance boom, when designer colognes dominated department store counters, Acqua di Giò caught on like wildfire, appealing to just about every kind of guy, whether for the office or date night. At its core is a beautifully nuanced blend of citrus, fresh marine accords, and soft florals, grounded by a musky amber base. On skin, it’s breezy, clean, and subtly woody, with an oceanic quality. If you’ve never rocked it or haven’t reached for it in years, do yourself a favor and revisit this classic.

Imitation is the highest form of flattery, and so many colognes still try to smell like Cool Water. Launched in 1988, it became a full-blown phenomenon in the ’90s, and for a generation of guys, it was practically a rite of passage. Along with CK One, it was non-negotiable during my formative years, and even then, before I’d developed my own distinct taste, I knew I didn’t want to smell like everyone else. But there was something about this intoxicating green aquatic I just couldn’t resist. Its blend of lavender, mint, rosemary, and neroli nodded to classic gentleman’s fougères, but Cool Water took that aromatic DNA somewhere new—a singular scent that’s herbal and richly marine, softened by a woody, musky warmth. While it might smell dated to some, there’s no denying its place among the most iconic fragrances of all time, and I’d argue it still smells amazing on the right dude, especially on a spring or summer day.

Terre d’Hermès is (probably) my favorite designer fragrance of all time. When Jean-Claude Ellena created it back in 2006, he delivered something entirely different from the crowd-pleasing designer colognes of the day. There’s an earthiness to it that I find irresistible, a marriage of citrus, dry woods, spice, and that unmistakable flinty, mineral character that gives it so much personality. It’s sophisticated without being stuffy, with a gorgeous, almost boozy warmth that makes it feel sultry and downright sexy. I particularly love wearing it in colder weather, when those warm, woody facets really come alive, but I can reach for it almost anytime. Plenty of designer colognes are simply pleasant, but Terre d’Hermès is distinctive and endlessly wearable.

Few colognes in modern history have generated as much conversation, inspired as many memes, or become quite as zeitgeist-y as Dior Sauvage. Love it or roll your eyes at its popularity, its influence on modern men’s perfumery is undeniable. Since its debut in 2015, Sauvage has become one of the world’s bestselling fragrances, at times even claiming the number-one spot. And it’s easy to see why. That unmistakable blend of citrus, spice, and all things ambery nice is crisp and fresh, with a warm, woody drydown that’s oh so smooth. It’s a crowd-pleaser in the truest sense, versatile enough to wear just about anywhere, though I think it really shines after dark. Sauvage has since spawned an entire family of flankers, but the original EDT started it all.

You've smelled Bleu de Chanel on plenty of guys. A beautifully composed citrus-spice-wood classic, it works just as well with a navy suit as it does with a white tee and jeans. Note: When Chanel's legendary perfumer Jacques Polge introduced it in 2010, he didn't just create another handsome, crowd-pleasing cologne; he helped define the modern blue fragrance, a fresh, clean, citrusy, and woody genre that's become a mainstay. Sixteen years on, the original remains one of the most approachable and endlessly versatile colognes ever. Its bright citrus opening gives way to an aromatic blend of cool mint, warming spices, and subtle florals, all grounded by a rich, woody base with touches of earthy vetiver, patchouli, and resinous warmth. There really is only one Bleu.

This was a tough call. Ask any scent head about Tom Ford's fragrances, and they’ll surely bring up Neroli Portofino and Tobacco Vanille, both arguably just as iconic (and good) as this one. But if you polled fans on the most influential Tom Ford fragrances, I think Oud Wood would edge out the competition. Launched in 2007, it helped introduce Oud to a broader Western audience, making the traditionally intense ingredient feel approachable. It’s elegant and beautifully blended, with a smoky, almost creamy heart of oud, sandalwood, and rosewood, accented by subtle spice and the warmth of vanilla and amber. It’s heady yet easy to wear, with an addictive richness that never wears thin.

I’ve worn pretty much every Le Labo under the sun, and while my personal favorites lean toward the eucalyptus and vetiver side of the house, there’s simply no telling the story of modern perfumery without Santal 33. Love it or find it utterly overplayed, you’ve smelled it. Since its 2011 debut, it’s wafted through elevators, the backseats of cabs, countless weddings and date nights, and just about everywhere in between. More importantly, it helped bring sandalwood into the mainstream, and became a reference point for an entire genre of warm, woody fragrances. But before everyone started rocking it, Santal 33 was, and still is, a brilliant composition: creamy sandalwood, dry cedar, cardamom spice, and leathery warmth. It’s a niche legend that has suffered from its own success, yes, but give it another ten years, and don’t be surprised if the very fragrance many got tired of smelling becomes cool all over again.

If you’re remotely a scent head, chances are you dig at least one, if not several, of Parfums de Marly’s fragrances (my personal favorite is the oud-praline magic that is Haltane). But if I had to sum up the house in one word, it would be regal. It does refined, layered elegance exceptionally well, and while some folks might champion Althaïr or Castley, to my nose, the fougère-forward Layton best epitomizes the house. Launched in 2016, it’s one of the finest fougères I’ve ever smelled, rich yet airy, with classic lavender reimagined alongside crisp apple, bright citrus, cardamom, woods, and a healthy dose of vanilla. It’s practically the template for what a modern fougère aspires to be, and its enduring popularity suggests plenty of fragrance fans would agree. It doesn’t hurt that the matte blue bottle with its signature silver dome is so flauntworthy.

Few fragrances in recent times have had the same cultural impact as Baccarat Rouge 540, becoming a signature scent for everyone from socialites to fragrance obsessives. Yes, it's polarizing, and some might argue its ubiquity has stripped it of some of its magic. But it's become a modern classic for a reason, starting with the masterful nose behind it: Francis Kurkdjian, founder of his namesake maison. Launched in 2015, it's a luminous floral amber, with saffron lending spice, jasmine bringing a soft warmth, and a generous dose of amberwood creating that glowing aura. Sultry, heady, and diffusive, it's a straight-up unisex phenomenon that smells a little different on everyone who wears it, yet still announces itself before you even enter a room. Whether you're a devotee or a detractor, there's no denying it's left its mark.

It came down to Bal d’Afrique and Gypsy Water, though plenty of Byredo fragrances could have earned a spot here. But I’m the editor, and I’m going with my all-time favorite from one of the houses that helped bring niche perfumery into the mainstream. Launched in 2008, Gypsy Water was one of the first niche fragrances I ever fell for, and it holds such a special place in my heart that I still wear it regularly. There’s something almost holy about its airy blend of incense, soft woods, bright lemon, and a whisper of vanilla and amber, all coming together with that subtle yet magnetic, almost skin-scent quality Byredo does so well. Artsy, chic, and easy to love, this woody aromatic never tries too hard to make an impression yet often leaves a lasting one.

Since its 2015 debut, Xerjoff’s Naxos has achieved near-mythic status, winning over everyone from fragrance-obsessed TikTokers to yacht-owning gentlemen with decidedly expensive taste. And I get it. This is an almost impossibly well-blended composition that somehow manages to be both decadent and incredibly wearable, making it a great place to start if you’re looking to venture into niche perfumery. On paper, the combination of tobacco, aromatic lavender, fruity freshness, and a prominent honey accord sounds like it shouldn’t quite work, but man, does it ever. That rich sweetness is a defining feature, especially in the opening, before the herbal, earthy tones and a hefty dose of vanilla come together in a downright sumptuous yet crisp way. The hype may have quieted down since its social media heyday, but Naxos deserves its flowers as a modern niche standout.

Halfeti has become a signature of mine, though I’m admittedly a little late to the game, having received my first bottle as a birthday gift last year, well after it had achieved iconic status in scent circles. But better late than never, especially when a fragrance is this good. Named after a Turkish town known for its roses, it leans into a rich, heady floral style, layered with citrus, herbs, and spice. Bergamot and grapefruit lift the opening before saffron and cardamom give way to a deep base of leather, oud, cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s a lot, but it all hangs together gorgeously, creating a woody, spicy, aromatic scent that’s elegant and sexy, perfect for special occasions or date nights. But I’d happily wear it just about anywhere, including when I’m not going anywhere at all.

Musc Ravageur embodies the risk-taking spirit of niche perfumery. Launched in 2000, it helped redefine what a modern musk fragrance could be at a time when fresh, clean fragrances dominated the men’s market. More than a quarter century later, it remains a cult favorite, thanks in no small part to its warm, almost funky (in a good way) richness. It opens with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and rose, all resting on a base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. A benchmark for animalic musks, it’s an alluring, sultry, and unapologetically sensual aroma, equally suited to being a signature scent or an olfactory companion for wherever the evening leads.

Amouage has dropped so many olfactory bangers over the years that choosing just one for this list wasn't easy. The Omani house has built its reputation on rich, complex compositions that keep you coming back to sniff your pulse points, and while I could make a case for several of its fragrances, Reflection Man feels quintessentially Amouage. Launched in 2007, it’s become a luxury niche benchmark, proving that a floral-forward fragrance can be every bit as rich and sophisticated as its woody or spicy counterparts. It opens with an herbaceous blend of rosemary, berries, and orange before orris, jasmine, and ylang-ylang bring a lush, earthy depth, all grounded by a smooth base of vetiver, patchouli, and sandalwood. The result is a layered floral-woody scent that’s distinctive without being difficult to wear, and versatile enough for everything from a boardroom to a black-tie gala. Pricey, yes, but worth every spritz.

#6565. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6564. Kit Keenan & Gigi Powers’s Mom’s Feta Artichoke Dip

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

Alongside her many talents, one quality I particularly applaud my mom for is her expertise in hosting. She is specifically known for what she dubbed “the emergency dinner party.” This is the kind of soirée that, despite being quickly organized—perhaps after a long day at work or a busy weekend afternoon—never fails to keep guests entertained and impressed. When it comes to appetizers at an emergency dinner party, the objective is to use limited ingredients, ensure ease of assembly, and deliver bangin’ flavor. For my mom’s famous feta artichoke dip, only three ingredients are absolutely crucial: feta, artichoke hearts, and olive oil. The brine from the canned artichoke hearts allows the feta to melt down in the oven, which in turn coats the artichoke hearts, creating a velvety dip. The best part about this recipe is that it’s completely customizable. My favorite variation includes adding honey, thyme, and an olive topper, which elevates the dip to a whole new level. Serve it with crunchy crostini or pita chips at your next dinner party, and your guests will go crazy.

#6563. Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor

Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor

With a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#6562. Photographer Franco Rubartelli Shares the Stories Behind Some of Vogue’s Most Famous ‘60s Shoots

Franco Rubartelli and Veruschka on location in Brazil.

Editor’s Note: Veruschka, the most super of ’60s models, has died. Her love affair with Franco Rubartelli played out in the pages of Vogue. In memoriam we are revisiting this interview with the photographer who wrote of Veruschka on Instagram: “She wasn’t just a great model. She was an elegant woman, sensitive, brave, with a beauty that did not stay in the camera, it would get into the soul of whoever watched her. She had a way of being in the world that you don't learn; you take in. People like Veruschka don’t go away at all. They stay in a picture, in a perfume, in a song, in a way of smiling.”

The 1960s were a heady time of change and youth and fantasy. This was also the case in Vogue, then led by Diana Vreeland, who brought her own taste for historicism and exoticism to its pages. “For Vreeland, everything impossible was possible,” says Franco Rubartelli, who, between 1964 and 1970, created some of the most memorable photographs ever published in the magazine. Presented in multipage spreads and taken in far-flung locales, these now-iconic images are exemplars of an elevated and romanticized hippie ethos. On a personal level, they documented one of fashion’s great love affairs.

Rubartelli, born in Florence, is a self-taught photographer who had planned to follow his father into the Italian Navy. He was pursuing his back-up plan, diplomacy, when Cupid arranged a collision that eventually steered him toward fashion. Enrolled at Cambridge to study English, Rubartelli recounts, he went to a pub to meet a blind date—who stood him up. As he rose to leave, he collided with a waitress carrying a tray of beer, which doused him. The tray bearer in question was a Swiss beauty named Françoise Schluter, earning pocket money at the pub while studying languages at the university. It was amore, and soon Rubartelli and Schluter were a couple. They married and lived in Rome with their son, Luigi. Tall, lithe, and blonde, Schluter was discovered on the streets there and started modeling. Her career transformed Rubartelli, by his own admission, into the archetypal jealous husband.

With her “scrubbed good looks,” Françoise Rubartelli models “American Sports Clothes in Italy.”

One night, after having mysteriously found a camera in their apartment, Rubartelli asked Schluter to pose for him on a beach. With no stylist, hair, or makeup—nor much knowledge of how the camera worked—he took pictures of the wife he feared he was losing, pictures that were infused with longing, youth, and freedom—qualities rarely expressed in the formal fashion photographs of the time. Having asked Schluter what the most important magazine was, Rubartelli got together some money to develop the film and secretly sent the results to Vogue.

Much to Rubartelli’s surprise, he received a positive reply from New York in the form of a telegram, signed Diana Vreeland, then Vogue’s editor in chief, that read: “Beautiful model, beautiful pictures, will get in touch with you.” Soon, the photographer and his model wife were working with Consuelo Crespi, the magazine’s editor in Rome; their first story appeared in the August 1964 issue. As Rubartelli and Schluter were racking up credits and becoming known as a couple, though, their love story was unraveling. “We spent too much time together as photographer and model, and not enough as man and woman,” Rubartelli explains via email. Their final rupture (circa 1965) left Rubartelli “without work, without my wife, without my model, without my son.”

Another no-show launched the second chapter of Rubartelli’s Vogue career. Having received a call about an advertising job, the young photographer went to meet the client at the Parco dei Principi Grand Hotel in Rome. He remembers that as he waited, and waited some more, “a tall, skinny woman in a black cloak and long knee-high boots walked past and caught my attention.” Rubartelli asked the concierge who she was and was told she was a German model, at which point he called his mother and asked her to pose as his secretary and invite this alluring Vera von Lehndorff-Steinort, aka Veruschka, to stop by his studio with her portfolio. “At this point,” Rubartelli explains, “my name was known through my work for Vogue. Veruschka stopped by in the early afternoon and we talked until the evening. I invited her to dinner at a restaurant. We spoke about Françoise, and she told me about her family. We shared our problems and stayed talking like two parrots until an innkeeper told us it was closing time. It was very late. We spent the rest of that night and every successive night together for nearly nine years. It was love at first sight.”

Theirs was a creative relationship that flourished in print and in life and took the pair around the globe. Recently Rubartelli, now living in Venezuela, has started to use Instagram as a biographical platform. Having spent endless hours poring over ’60s Vogues and becoming especially curious about Rubartelli and his models, his Instagram diary left me spellbound and eager to know more. I reached out to the ebullient Rubartelli, who openly and graciously agreed to share some personal stories with me.

“You know something?” Rubartelli recently wrote, “I think that I have never been a photographer. I was simply a man who loved the two most important women of his life through his camera. I remember how beautiful my pictures came out when I was in love with Françoise or Veruschka, and when our stories ended, when there was no more feeling between us, I could stay for hours and hours in front of them without doing one good picture.” Rubartelli does himself a disservice. The Vogue archive provides evidence that he very much has a feeling for the form.

Here, the stories behind some of his best-known Vogue assignments.

“[After meeting and falling in love], we decided to take some photos together. Veruschka was very tall—her size was not commercial for the fashionable photos at that time—so we got to thinking about doing something different, and we came up with the idea of body painting. No one had been doing this.”

“We bought colorful makeup, feathers, and paillettes and decided, on our own dime, to go to the island of Eleuthera in the Bahamas. There we painted Veruschka’s naked body.”

“During the time we shared together, I noticed that Veruschka carried with her inferiority complexes from her childhood. It sometimes felt as if she were not happy in her body, that her personality wanted to evade its physical dimension to become other beings. She found in makeup the possibility of escaping and transforming into other things: a butterfly that could fly, a panther or a tiger to run in the jungle, a mermaid to sink into the sea.”

“We often went to Veruschka’s mother’s house in Petersrkirchen, near Munich. She was a very open-minded lady and very proud of Vera. She lived in a big house with many rooms. When we visited, our rooms were under the roof on the second floor. They were very big and all built in wood.”

“Veruschka’s mother lived a drama with all her daughters during the Second World War. Her husband, [Heinrich Graf von Lehndorff-Steinort], participated in the plot to kill Hitler in his bunker. It was not successful, and he was executed. [According to Der Spiegel, Vera’s mother, Gottliebe, was first put in prison and then placed in a working camp with her newborn child. Her older daughters were moved, with other children of the resistance, to a nursing home and renamed.] Reunited after the war, they moved from one place to another and were very poor. When I met Vera’s mother, she had a boyfriend living with her. He was a crazy musician playing very heavy and noisy music. Her mother loved him and his music. In winter, the place was very beautiful. It was near a forest, and the fog made a great atmosphere.” From left: Countesses Catharina and Vera (known as Veruschka) von Lehndorff, Frau Marie Eleonora von Haeften, and Baroness Gabriela von Plotho.

“The Queen Christina assignment came about while we were watching the movie [about her] starring the tremendous Greta Garbo. Before the film was over, Veruschka and I simultaneously had the idea to propose the look of the queen to Diana Vreeland. Enthusiastic, we asked for an appointment with her and got one for the following week. This meant that we had to work day and night without sleeping to have the project ready with sketches. If we weren’t on time, we’d have to wait a long time to see her. We were always a little nervous about what Mrs. Vreeland’s reaction would be. She was a very straight woman; if she liked an idea, she would accept it right away; if she didn’t like it, we understood immediately that the project did not work for Vogue. She was very fond of us, but didn’t care about our reaction if she did not like the idea.”

“Mrs. Vreeland’s mysterious office [was infused] with the smell of her candle. How she walked, how she moved her hands with her long, expressive fingers, was very exotic. She created a magical atmosphere in her office, which had black walls full of photographs and furniture upholstered in an intense red fabric, mixed with leopard skins. In this dim environment you almost didn’t see Vreeland, who dressed all in black and red and almost matched the decor. ‘How are you, Mrs. Vreeland?’ asked Veruschka. We explained all the details and she listened in silence. It was a silence that was scary. Finally, when we finished, she got to her feet and congratulated us, saying: ‘This is so fabulous; let’s do it!’”

“Mrs. Vreeland loved the Queen Christina idea and ordered dresses to be made for Veruschka. We headed to Austria, where we made Innsbruck our base. For 10 days we looked for locations. It wasn’t easy to find a castle.”

“Mrs. Vreeland almost never rejected an idea: Queen Christina, Libya, Texas, Australia, Brazil . . . . For Vreeland, everything impossible was possible, and she didn’t put limits on our creativity. This was very stimulating for us, because every project we proposed was more daring. I remember one time she called us by surprise and asked us to go to Rio de Janeiro to photograph some dresses during Carnival. She showed us the clothes and explained her idea to us. ‘Franco,’ she said, ‘I do not want to see the Carnival; I want you to work in a studio with the windows opened. Franco,’ she continued, ‘I want, I want . . . pissst.’ She made a buzzing noise with her mouth closed. ‘I want you to shoot like that. Do you understand what I mean?’ I did not. It was impossible to understand what she meant with that sound.”

“I think Mrs. Vreeland was very original. Having such an important position in the world of fashion in those years, she directed taste toward the different, the eccentric. She understood things immediately, and if she liked an idea, she approved it on the spot. She had very precise ideas about colors; for example, she loved red and dressed in it and decorated her apartment in it. Apart from her strong and precise ideas of color, one could never be sure about her decisions until the last moment. Once she liked an idea and authorized it, she approved the costs of the productions. There was never an intention to reduce the result by making any kind of economy.”

“I can assure you, without a doubt, that Veruschka, myself, and Giorgio di Sant’Angelo [a textile designer turned stylist and designer] were a creative team for a long period. We met together to develop themes, and if we had a trip that we liked, we gave ourselves to the story until we fully developed it. Veruschka and I really enjoyed going to Giorgio’s house. We spent many hours there thinking, drawing ideas, doing tests. Then, back in the city, we visited museums, bought books to study, saw films, all to perfect our ideas and to make sure of the look that we wanted to create.”

“Giorgio [above right] was unlike anyone else; his creativity was superior. He had been born in Florence, Italy, but had spent so much time outside of the country that he had forgotten the language a little; when he spoke, it was a funny [argot]. He was an original and very imaginative designer. Giorgio was an excellent companion also in private life. He shared with his friends the joyful moments as well as the anxious ones and tried to creative a positive atmosphere. His style tended toward the exotic. His only defect was that he smoked too much; he was never without a cigarette in his hand. He was an artist in creating jewelry, and he himself was upholstered in necklaces of all kinds.”

“Giorgio loved colors and their mixture. I studied him as we prepared for our journey to the Painted Desert. In order to decide what fabrics to bring with us, he came to the studio with many samples of all colors. In front of a mirror he tested the various combinations by cutting and mixing the different pieces with incredible taste and perfection. It was fun to see him. He looked like a scarecrow all covered in pieces of cloth. For the final test shots on Veruschka, he invented the gypsy look by cutting all sorts of fabrics and wrapping them around the body.”

“When we decided to work in the desert of Libya, we visited many stores looking for fabrics suitable for all the drapings that would be made on location. They weren’t sewn dresses, but draped on the body. We were creating a look, an atmosphere—nothing more. We went to Diana Vreeland to sell her an atmosphere, and she accepted it and gave us carte blanche. Of course, we had our sketches, but sometimes we were moved by feelings, or so inspired by the atmosphere, that we were forced to change things.”

“Every morning in one location or another, Veruschka, almost naked, was standing for many hours as Giorgio draped on her body. These preparations were incredible. In the sand around us there were meters of fabric that Giorgio cut and adapted to her body. We had a long mirror that Veruschka could see herself in. Although we always started early in the morning, before dawn, these preparations lasted many hours, and I worried and complained because the light became too strong. We couldn’t work later than 10:00 a.m.; we could start again after 4:00 p.m. when the desert light turned gold.”

“I remember that when we traveled, Giorgio spent a lot of time researching, trying to find original clothes typical of each place we were visiting. Before our shoot in Ghadames, he went to visit the small souk of the town, where he discovered two small warehouses full of typical desert fabrics and bought many of them. As he did not have much money, he made a deal with the store owner, agreeing to swap the fabrics he had brought for the ones in the souk, so Giorgio returned to New York with stupendous finds.”

“Giorgio came to the desert shoot every day with two or three suitcases full of fabrics that he modeled on Veruschka’s body according to his state of mind. He spread the fabrics out on the ground so he could have a panoramic view of them all. One day a strong breeze blew in all of a sudden and the fabrics began to fly away. It was amusing to see Giorgio run after them in the dunes, and suddenly stumble and fall. Once we were approached by a little girl from Ghadames. She was very cute and watched us curiously. After a while she grabbed a piece of fabric and put it on her head, simulating what Giorgio was doing with Veruschka. We asked her not to touch and to go away, but Giorgio stopped what he was doing with Veruschka and draped some fabric on her, then he cut the cloth and let the girl run away with ‘a custom Giorgio di Sant’Angelo.’”

#6561. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday both deliver a plethora of deals, but they play a little differently. Big-name retailers and legacy brands usually kick things off on Black Friday, while smaller menswear boutiques tend to hold their fire until Cyber Monday. Expect solid discounts starting around 20% off—and keep your eyes peeled for the coveted sale-on-sale action that’s become the norm in recent years.

#6559. This $20 Gadget Is My Grandpa’s Secret To Making Big-Batch Potatoes For The Holidays

It looks a little ridiculous, but I can’t stop watching it work.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Growing up, there was one thing I could always count on: If I expressed even a hint of interest in something my grandpa had, I’d have my very own on my doorstep the minute I returned home... and so would every other member of our family. That’s how we became a family full of Rotatos.

If you don’t know what a Rotato is, allow me to introduce you. This rather bare-bones machine will seamlessly peel your potatoes (and other fruits and veggies, too) in just seconds—and the entertainment value is off the charts.

One day while I was visiting my grandparents, I watched my grandfather use his Rotato to peel enough potatoes for a large batch of latkes, then fry up all the peels. His giant batches allowed him to freeze his latkes and enjoy them for months on end. But why spend time peeling all those potatoes yourself when you could whip out a handy gadget that does it all for you?

The Rotato is a mesmerizing device. Sure, it’s a single-use kitchen product, but I could literally watch this baby peel things for hours. Since I first expressed my awe and received one of my very own (along with my parents, sister, and cousins), I’ve tried the Rotato on all kinds of produce.

Mangos? No problem. Apples? Easy as 1-2-3. Any time I’m making a dish that needs something peeled in bulk, the Rotato is my go-to gadget. And my entire family has hopped on board.

Using it reminds me of putting on a record. You simply place your potato (or veggie of choice) on the spike at the bottom of the device, lower the top spike to hold it in place, and position the peeling blade against the top of the potato. Just press the red button, and the machine does the rest, automatically stopping when the cutter arm reaches the bottom.

And once you’ve watched it tackle a potato, it’s hard not to wonder what other fruits and vegetables you can try next.

According to the Rotato’s instruction manual, it can also peel cucumbers, beets, turnips, avocados, eggplants, squash, zucchini, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, kiwis, lemons, limes, and oranges—way more than I even imagined. I’ll have to start dreaming up new recipes.

Since discovering the magic of the Rotato, I’ve used it to make mashed potatoes for Friendsgiving, fruit salad, and much more. Sure, it doesn’t get used consistently year-round, but when you’re cooking for a crew, it’s the handiest thing in the kitchen.

#6558. Sheet-Pan Cider Vinegar Chicken

Slashing bone-in chicken thighs (carefully, around the bone, of course) allows a punchy maple-Dijon-ACV marinade to permeate the meat deeply in a short amount of time. And that waiting time is well spent: Scatter torn sourdough bread on a baking sheet and bake until crisp, then toss croutons aside to make way for the thighs. Once the chicken is cooked through, toss the croutons in the rendered fat and cook until everything is bronzed and glistening. A few handfuls of arugula make an elegant finish—who needs a side salad?

Whisk 5 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup plus 3 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar, 5 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 3 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) in a measuring glass or small bowl to combine. Transfer 2 Tbsp. vinegar mixture to a small bowl; set aside.

Arrange 3 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (6–8), skin side up, on a cutting board. Season lightly with salt. Turn over and season lightly on other side with salt, then carefully use a sharp paring knife to make 3 long slashes, going most of the way through meat (avoid the bone). Transfer to a large bowl and pour vinegar mixture in measuring glass over. Toss chicken to coat, making sure to get liquid into slashes. Let chicken sit at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour.

Meanwhile, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 8 oz. country-style or sourdough bread (about ⅓ loaf), torn into 1" pieces, on a rimmed baking sheet. Drizzle remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and sprinkle with a pinch of salt and a pinch of freshly ground black pepper; toss to coat. Arrange bread in a single layer and bake until golden, 12–15 minutes. Transfer croutons to a plate; reserve baking sheet.

Arrange reserved chicken on reserved baking sheet and nestle 3 large shallots, quartered lengthwise through root ends, around; pour any excess vinegar mixture in bowl over. Bake chicken until golden, cooked through, and an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part, avoiding bone, registers at least 165° (it should be well over), 25–30 minutes.

Scatter croutons over empty areas of baking sheet and toss to soak up juices. Roast until chicken and croutons are deeply browned, 10–12 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes, then top with 2 oz. arugula and drizzle with reserved vinegar mixture in small bowl.

#6557. “The Most Beautitul Woman in the World…”: Richard Avedon’s Ode to Veruschka in 1972

TWO SPECTACULARS Veruschka, one of the great wonders of our time, here, with another: the Great Chrysanthemum Diamond, a remarkable 104.15 carats, made even more so by its color—a deep golden brown with flashes of orange, green, blue, and scarlet.

Editor’s note: Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort—the model best known as Veruschka—died on November 24, according to a report in the German tabloid Bild. She was 87.

Veruschka was a frequent presence in the pages of Vogue throughout the 1960s and ’70s, appearing on the cover at least a dozen times and posing for photographers including Irving Penn, Franco Rubartelli, Horst P. Horst, Bert Stern, and Richard Avedon, who considered her a muse.

Indeed, in 1972, Avedon penned a tribute to Veruschka, the ur-supermodel, for Vogue’s May issue. We have reprinted that text—and the original captions, which breathlessly celebrate Veruschka’s famously lithe figure—here.

Veruschka is the most beautiful woman in the whole world. There’s just nobody like her. If she’s beautiful, she’s beautiful alone. There are imitations of Sophia Loren, only not as good, and a new Garbo is discovered every decade, but there is and will always be only one Veruschka. Beauty isolates the person who owns it and isolation makes demands on the imagination. Veruschka’s bones, her body, her extraordinary length have compelled her to invent her own person. There’s just no one she could imitate.

There’s never enough of her. Each encounter is unfulfilled and unforgettable. It has nothing to do with ordinary life. The last time I photographed her she said, “Goodbye for now,” and then she didn’t come back for five years. When she finally walked in, I felt as if we’d both been waiting every day of those years between. I couldn’t disappoint her.

I love looking at her through the dressing-room door. It’s usually pretty crowded in there and she sits at the dressing table with her tea and honey, naked, oblivious to hairdressers, fashion editors and assistants, making up her face with a Japanese paintbrush. She has the concentration of a child playing some totally private, wordless game alone as she places the shadows where she wants them and the highlights where she thinks they belong.

She chooses words very carefully. She talks about her skin as if it has a mind of its own. It can be tired when she’s not. She speaks of her hair as a head of independent hairs and calls them “my hairs,” even the baby ones at the back of her neck. And that’s not a grammatical error. It has to do with consideration.

VITALITY…VERUSCHKA EXPLODES WITH IT Flying mane, flashing smile, Veruschka lighting up the day in her own bright white pants suit, black-and-white shirt and boots. … She is, quite simply, an extraordinary natural beauty. Like other great beauties, she insists upon a régime aimed at keeping those looks, that fantastic energy at their peak... part of Veruschka’s program, next pages.... Suit and shirt, by Antony Arland; boots, by Nazareno Gabrielli. All, designed especially for Veruschka. Scarf by Halston.

She’ll cover her breasts in front of some and not in front of others. That selectivity has implications of intimacy and trust. It’s a commitment. She’s sensitive to the fact that she’s undressed and you’re there and it’s full of nuances which she will neither deny nor resolve. They become resolved in the work.

I love talking with her because of that voice. There’s none like it, deep, unimaginably soft, and, for a romantic girl, remarkably unsentimental, which gives romance its real power. She knows the value of a quiet, two-hour conversation before going on the set. The time is never wasted. Her skin is like litmus paper for her feelings. She’s all made up and ready and, as we sit together, her skin gets very warm in color and then, suddenly, it drains. The second the color leaves her face, I know she’s ready to work.

Veruschka is the only woman I permit to look at herself in the mirror while I’m photographing her. The mirror makes most women aware of their weaknesses and, in trying to correct them, they come up with evasions, hiding arms that seem too thin or hips that seem too wide. Veruschka knows that it is what’s peculiar to her that’s beautiful and she works to bring it forward. It’s wonderful to see her searching for and emphasizing her irregularities.

EXERCISE...VERUSCHKA’S SARAN SAUNA, HER MIRACLE TUBE-STRETCH Clinging coats of Dow’s Saran Wrap around her body, Veruschka, opposite, wrapped for exercise. Within half an hour, this individual sauna has forced the body to shed more tissue-locked water than a real sauna could have done. Same technique can be used on any problem area—upper arms, thighs, waist—of any body, even one in such enviable shape as Veruschka’s. This was hit upon by top-notch Manhattan gymnast and exercise director Venizelos Antoniadis... Left, the two-way-stretch exercise tube designed by Giorgio di Sant’ Angelo in the marvelous Patternskin fabric that he developed from Du Pont’s Antron nylon and Lycra for United Elastic. The dress has its own Dr. Denton-like feel, and stretching in it is “like working against a wall”—but when not stretching as here, “it falls beautifully, very cloudy and soft,” says Giorgio.

There are times during a sitting when she turns to look at me or at the camera and, without so much as lifting an eyebrow or curving her mouth, smiles, challenges. It’s like the opposite of the Dylan song, “I’ll let you in my dream if you’ll let me in yours.” That seems to be what most people need. But not Veruschka. She’ll let you look into her dream but she wouldn’t fit in yours.

There’s a profoundly moving moment at the end of every sitting with Veruschka when I say, “I think I’ve got it.” She looks at me with a startled expression that comes very quickly across her face. I once asked her what she hopes for from a sitting, why she does it, and she said, “When I was a child I loved things because they were beautiful, but that isn’t enough. I want to do something with it. You make photographs. I would like to do it with my own body. I’m fascinated to see myself reproduced again, that there is no end of looking always a little bit different. And this is like a wine or a drug or something. You always have to have another one.” Ending the sitting, which is something only I can do, is like an interruption. I feel as if I’m taking her away from work that, for her, will always be unfinished.

YOGA...FOR SERENITY OF MIND, FOR LIMBERNESS OF BODY Veruschka puts her incredible body through the slow motions of advanced yoga under the guidance of the renowned Swami Satchidananda. Top left, the Ardha Matsyendrasana or half spiral twist. Top right, a variation of the Supta Vojrasana, or bent pelvic pose. Bottom right, the Sarvangasana, or shoulder stand, and, most strikingly, above, the Yoga Nidrasana, or yogic sleep pose. Her diaper-wrap yoga suit, in cashmere-like Nomelle yarn of Orlon, by Giorgio di Sant’ Angelo.

It’s impossible to be beautiful without being moving and impossible to be moving without a sense of irony. Veruschka makes me laugh a lot. She makes everybody laugh. At her most remarkable, when everything is perfect and the light is on her and we are all frozen by what she has accomplished, she sinks a little deeper into her knees, looks at my assistant holding the light, and says, “He makes good lightning, no?”

It is both deliberate and a little hesitant. She keeps you guessing about how much she really knows. She seems to hover, waiting for the laughter. It’s the subtlest kind of demand. It’s not just that she’s said something funny. She’s made you want to laugh for her.

She turns words around. She turns everything around. Her presence in a room calls it all into question, what you thought you knew, what you were sure of. Nothing looks the same as it did before she got there. Tall girls become short girls. Brown walls go golden. Being beautiful in her way demands something and you must extend yourself to meet the challenge or know that a kind of splendor is lost to you forever.

THIS IS WHAT IT’S ALL ABOUT...TO LOOK LIKE THIS After all the exercise, the polishing, the yoga—the knockout punch of Veruschka at night. The relaxed, alive beauty of radiant skin and gleaming hair; the end that more than justifies the means. The bias black silk crêpe dress, left, the sexiest bared black dress in a season of sexy, bare, black dresses. By Stavropoulos, of Peter Griffin silk. Black coil bracelet by Paul Iwao. Ring, of exquisitely matched pieces of marble cone shell encased in gold, by Marguerite Stix for Cartier, Veruschka’s coif by Ara Gallant.

#6556. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6555. 21 Easy Thanksgiving Appetizers That Make Hosting A Breeze

Thanksgiving asks a lot of us (and our ovens!). From making the turkey to all of the casseroles and sides, don’t even get me started on dessert. You’ve got a lot on your plate, so we’re trying to make the big turkey day a little easier. Appetizers are my favorite part of the meal: little bites that pack so much flavor and fun into the start of the big feast, so you’ve gotta make them count. We’ve got some clever, simple shortcuts to help you whip up appetizers that will impress your guests without adding to your stress.

Whether you’re looking for quick and easy last-minute options or want something more elaborate, we’ve got something on this list for you. Need more Thanksgiving hosting ideas? Check out our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes and Thanksgiving cocktails!

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer to serve during the holidays. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie. Add a bit of fresh thyme and some roasted pecans, and you’ve got yourself a certified crowd-pleaser.

There is nothing better than a soft, homemade dinner roll. These rolls use sweet potatoes to make them even softer and fluffier, similar to our classic potato rolls. These would be a fun alternative to biscuits or Parker House rolls at Thanksgiving or another big family meal.

Having multiple Thanksgivings this year? Want to transform your leftovers from one into something incredible for the next? Look no further than this stuffed bread ring—it's gorgeous and super easy, thanks to store-bought crescent roll dough.

With all of the elements of stuffing plus the added flaky and butter benefits of biscuits, this pull-apart stuffing bread just might start a tug-of-war situation at your table when you grab for a slice.

It’s a tail as old as time: It’s right before Thanksgiving dinner, and your guests don’t want a full meal but are feeling a little peckish. Try a bird of a different feather this year, and serve this festive and impressive fruit and cheese display as the centerpiece of your holiday app table.

These Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. Preparing these potato skins is simple; all you need for this recipe are Thanksgiving leftovers and a few additional pantry staples: potatoes and cheddar cheese.

It’s hard to find a party appetizer that’s more beloved than a cheese log—or its alternate form, the cheese ball. Here, dried sweetened cranberries, walnuts, and fresh thyme conjure a holiday feeling, while a little honey complements the sweet-tart fruit.

These are a fan favorite every fall. They always disappear within minutes, probably because the combo of salty, creamy brie, sweet-tart cranberry sauce, and crunchy pecans is PERFECT.

Fall desserts may get all the attention once autumn comes around, but I'm here to say that seasonal appetizers deserve their share of the spotlight—especially these adorable pizza-stuffed pumpkins. Stuffed with creamy ricotta, these biscuit-based bites are baked to golden perfection before being brushed with a flavor-packed garlic butter.

Just like our famous cranberry brie bites, these little guys are hard to put down! They're the perfect amount of sweet and savory, so you can serve them before or after the big meal.

Sausage Stuffing Bites With Cranberry Sauce

Stuffing, inside the turkey or out, is a Thanksgiving staple. The only thing better? MORE. STUFFING. Enter this bite-sized, stuffing-centered appetizer with a tangy, three-ingredient dipping sauce (just cranberry sauce, honey, and Dijon).

Even if you're not serving turkey this Thanksgiving doesn't mean you can't get in on the theme. Enter: this adorable cheeseball. We used carrots, pecans, pretzels, and bell peppers to create the iconic look, but feel free to substitute them with different ingredients for what you have on hand. Serve it with crackers and use the decorations as dippers too!

These sweet potato bites have a crunchy, herbaceous crust, with a sweet, silky inside that, when topped with a light drizzle of honey, will have you craving them again and again. Once you bite through the crust, the sweet potato mixes with that melted, nutty Gruyère for a dream flavor combination that works SO well.

Cranberry brie bites are by far one of our favorite appetizers for the holidays, but jalapeño poppers also have place in our hearts too... So why not combine them? The spice of the jalapeño goes so well with the tart cranberries.

To make these, we stuff baby bella mushrooms with garlicky, herby breadcrumbs and plenty of cheese. Stuff them ahead of time and bake them off when you're ready for the most Thanksgiving-friendly appetizer ever.

Pull-apart bread reaches a whole new level, thanks to brie and cranberry sauce. Use your favorite homemade sauce recipes, but store-bought works too if you're short for time.

Little puff pastry squares get topped with caramelized onions and a little crumbled goat cheese for an easy appetizer that always wows. The final step is a light drizzle of honey for that salty sweet combination everyone will love.

If you’re a fan of our cranberry brie bites, we’ve got news for you: There’s a new app in town, and it’s inspired by another fan fave, baked feta pasta. These features the flavors you know and love, all nestled into bite-sized cups of golden crescent roll dough.

There's something very classic about the crescent roll dough flavor, so we tend to gravitate toward it, but puff pastry or even biscuit dough should both work here, too.
