#6386. The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

Basing entire business plans on back-of-the-envelope calculations might not seem like the best idea. However, according to a new paper available in preprint on arXiv by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, that is precisely what the companies touting orbital AI data centers are doing. While on paper, the math looks good, the physical constraints of actually utilizing all the processing power and free energy of the Sun that orbit provides is prohibitive in a number of ways - and it will be a long time before we have the technology to truly capitalize on the advantages of space-based AI.

First, letâs dig into what the back-of-the-envelope calculations say. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory suggests that U.S.-based data centers could consume 580 terawatt-hours of electricity over a five-year window, an increase of around 17-46 gigawatts compared to modern levels. But land-based data centers are running into plenty of bottlenecks, from newly elected hostile politicians to hard caps on the electrical gridâs ability to supply all that additional power.

So the solution seems obvious - launch the data centers into orbit, where they will be beyond any individual NIMBY protesters, have access to essentially unlimited free solar power, and not have to deal with water cooling systems. Sounds pretty good. Until the actual physics of what that means comes into play.

Fraser addresses the idea of data centers in space.

There are three main physics hurdles that all culminate into a giant economic one facing data centers, and it all comes down to scale. Size and weight are the first major obstacle. Dr. Turyshev uses a baseline 1-megawatt orbital processing facility as an example. It would hold roughly the processing power of a small commercial server room. But in space it would require 5,640 square meters of deployed solar panels, even in a âdawn-duskâ orbit designed to minimize the time it spends in Earthâs shadow. Thatâs roughly the size of an American football field.

On top of that, the spacecraft would need around 2,500 square meters of radiator panels to stop the electronics from frying themselves. Combining the power generation and cooling equipment required would already bring a spacecraft up to 30 metric tons. Adding in structural trusses, control thrusters, and radiation shielding brings the total mass of 1 MW of orbital data capacity is likely between 34 and 59 metric tons.

For the purposes of practicality, Dr. Turyshev then drops down to a 100 kW center, since a 1 MW data center would not even fit in many modern rocket fairings. Arguably, since each 100 kW data center wouldnât be exactly 10% of the weight of a 1 MW data center, he uses a rough estimate of around 5 metric tons for a single spacecraft of that size. The problem is, to keep up with demand, we would need to launch between 170,000 and 461,000 of them over the course of five years. And each Falcon 9 can only launch at most four of them. That would require almost 9,000 Falcon 9 launches over the next five years - or roughly 33 of them per week.

Fraser talks about turning the Moon into a data center.

Even if we had the launch capacity for that sheer scale, there is another bottleneck to contend with - getting the data back to Earth. As we reported earlier this week, weâve made great strides in high-speed optical communications down from orbit lately. However, the headline number of 200 gigabits per second is a single point in time. These âhigh speedâ links realistically deliver around 13 to 26 gigabits per second continuously, in part because they require a direct line of sight to the ground station theyâre communicating with, and they also canât communicate through clouds. Even if we flooded major parts of the Earthâs surface with ground stations, those speeds would severely hobble any interactive cloud apps or data-heavy training runs that require continual syncing with anything on the ground.

But even if we solved the communications problem, thereâs still the problem of that omnipresent menace in space - radiation. Cosmic rays are famous for flipping single bits in computer memory, constantly forcing processors to run error-checking algorithms, and thereby eating into usable computer time. According to the paper, over a five-year mission, the cumulative radiation damage and micrometeoroid impacts would continually degrade both the electronics and solar panels, driving up the cost of every calculation completed.

With all that in mind, the economic hurdle becomes very clear. On Earth, a high-end AI data center costs between $10,000 and $40,000 per kilowatt of computing capacity. In order for a 40-kilogram per kilowatt orbital satellite to match that pricing, it would need combined launch and manufacturing costs of between $250 and $1,000 per kilogram. For comparison, current dedicated Falcon 9 launches work out to roughly $3,360 per kilogram. So the launch cost alone is three to thirteen times more expensive than the entire combined launch and manufacturing cost of a single data center.

Video from Astraveo arguing the same physics as what Dr. Turyshev talks about in the paper. Credit - Astraveo YouTube Channel

With all that said, there are some niche applications for orbital computing in the near future, according to the paper. The first is space-native processing, where satellites crunch the raw imagery for Earth-observation satellites or sensor data before broadcasting high-value insights back down to Earth. Another is communications-based edge computing, where processors piggyback on existing constellations like Starlink that already pay for solar arrays, lasers, and ground stations.

But ultimately, despite this paper, various organizations are moving forward with their plans for data centers in orbit. Even today (November 25th) the FCC approved SpaceXâs application to launch one million âStarmindâ orbital data centers by 2040. Earlier this month, Google booked a flight on a Blue Origin rocket for a test of its Project Suncatcher computing constellation. Until the real economics of the situation catch up with them, it might be a while before these efforts realize what hard physical limits theyâre going up against.

S. G. Turyshev - Orbital Data Centers: Spacecraft Constraints and Economic Viability

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope followed up on years-old observations to confirm the first recorded act of a giant star swallowing its companion. The stellar cannibalism occurred just next door, in the Andromeda galaxy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, astronomers have caught two stars — a supergiant and a star slightly smaller than the sun — in the act of merging. After orbiting each other for thousands of years, the pair came together in just under seven years — a span short enough that researchers could watch the drama play out from start to finish. The discovery was described in a study published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

"Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, said in a NASA statement. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do."

The stars' imminent merger was originally picked up by NASA's now-retired Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer — a spacecraft that was designed to spot asteroids but also discovered many other interesting changes in the night sky.

Researchers noticed that a previously stable binary star system in the Andromeda galaxy, the closest major galaxy to ours, had begun to brighten. Follow-up observations from the Wide-Field Infrared Transient Explorer ‪—‬ a near-infrared instrument at the Palomar Observatory in California — revealed that the galaxy had also started spewing dust. Karambelkar’s team backed up these observations with data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in December 2025.

The researchers dubbed the binary pair "Bao" (after its formal name, AT 2025abao) and started keeping tabs. They found that sometime in 2018, the smaller component of Bao bumped into the surface of the supergiant Bao. From there, things escalated quickly. The stars started exchanging gas in a process known as common envelope evolution. The larger Bao dragged its smaller companion closer and closer, until it was finally sucked into the supergiant's core, releasing a gigantic burst of energy.

Views of the stellar merger in Andromeda (left) captured by the NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and James Webb space telescopes (right).

This dramatic culmination was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," study co-author Kishalay De, an astronomer at Columbia University, said in the statement.

The researchers were surprised by not only the speed of this interaction but also its outcome. Bao could have easily exploded into a supernova, transformed into a neutron star or collapsed into a black hole. Instead, it seems to have settled back into a single massive star. Future observations will give scientists a sense of how the new, rejuvenated Bao is holding up after its act of cosmic cannibalism.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team's analysis could also help inform future studies of supergiant stars and binary systems. Getting a clearer picture of how common envelope evolution works could allow astronomers to reconstruct how previous mergers went down. Thanks to NASA's new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, Karambelkar predicts Bao will be far from the last merging stars scientists spot.

#6384. Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

"It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?"

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently."

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”

"Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

#6383. The Event Horizon Telescope Views the Dynamics and Geometry of a Black Hole Jet in Extreme Detail

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a massive international collaboration of scientists and radio observatories, is like the gift that keeps on giving. In 2019, the EHT Collaboration gave us the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the heart of the M87 galaxy (M87*). In 2022, it provided the first image of Sagittarius A*, the SMBH at the center of the Milky Way. Between 2024 and 2026, the international array also produced detailed images of the relativistic jet emanating from 3C 84 and M87*.

Meanwhile, EHT observations in 2021 also resolved the innermost jet region of the blazar 3C 279 in unprecedented detail. These efforts, described in a paper that appeared in Astronomy & Astrophysics, revealed the jet's dynamics and geometry at sub-parsec scales, suggesting it bends toward Earth-based instruments on these scales. Combined with earlier EHT campaigns and multifrequency data, the EHT team's latest results are helping astronomers identify its nature and the mechanisms driving it.

By definition, blazars are bright galaxies with an SMBH at their centers - Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) - that have relativistic jets of ionized matter directed straight toward Earth. Located approximately 538 million light-years away, the jet coming from its center is powered by an SMBH with an estimated mass of about 800 million solar masses (by comparison, Sagittarius A* is about 4.3 million solar masses). Because of its brightness, 3C 279 is considered a prime target for Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) and is frequently used for calibration.

An image of the core region of Messier 87, a supermassive black hole, processed from an array of radio telescopes known as the EHT with colours indicating brightness temperature (Credit: Event Horizon Telescope)

The 2021 campaign represents the largest EHT array configuration published to date, with the addition of two new sites. These were the 12-m telescope at the Kitt Peak Observatory in Arizona and the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) interferometer in the French Alps. These additions provided crucial intermediate baselines that significantly improved coverage, especially at intermediate scales, enabling constraints on specific angular scales. These constraints were essential for probing both compact and extended structures in the jet.

Hendrik MÃ¼ller, a staff scientist in the Data Management and Software (DMS) group at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO) and a former researcher with the Max-Planck-Institut fÃ¼r Radioastronomie, was the lead author of the paper that appeared in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. As he told Universe Today via email, the EHT is continuously growing and adding more telescopes every year, including the Greenland Telescope in 2018. But as he noted, the Kitt Peak and NOEMA observatories were especially important to these observations:

The physical baseline between two antennas in the array determines the spatial scale that this baseline can resolve. That is, for example, the reason why the Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico is built on railway tracks: When you move the antennas closer to each other, you zoom out of the image and see the larger field of view.

If you move them closer to each other, you zoom into the image, achieve higher resolution, but see only a small view of the sky. The locations of the radio telescopes in the EHT could of course not be changed, but Kitt Peak and NOEMA were important because they are relatively close to other telescopes in the array (NOEMA in the French Alpes to Pico Veleta close to Granada, Spain. They added information that was not available to us in previous years.

To process the volumes of data gathered by the EHT arrays, the team relied on Comrade, DoG-HiT, kine, and Difmap imaging software, a strategy similar to the one used to reconstruct the famous M87 black hole image in 2019. As MÃ¼ller explained, the team used different software packages that make different assumptions about the image to build confidence in the result by checking for consistency across methods. Beyond imaging, many more collaborators and software were used during early data-processing steps, like correlation or calibration.

Illustration of the multiwavelength 3C 279 jet structure in April 2017. The observing epochs, arrays, and wavelengths are noted in each panel. Credit: J.Y. Kim/MPIfR/VLBA and GMVA/EHT

The results, as noted, suggest that the jet curves so that one section of it points closer to Earth. While the jet is already oriented towards our instruments, MÃ¼ller explained how this small change can have two visible effects:

Because the plasma is moving close to the speed of light, its radiation is concentrated in the direction it's traveling. When that direction lines up more closely with Earth, we see brighter emission. At the same time, features in the jet are moving more nearly straight toward us, so they can appear to move more slowly across the sky. Think of a car coming almost head-on: it can be moving fast while barely shifting left or right in your field of view.

That's what makes the bend a useful explanation for 3C 279. Farther along the inner jet, we see brighter emission and slower apparent motion. Both can result from a change in direction, even if the plasma keeps moving just as fast. That also means the brightest spot in the image can be downstream from the black hole, where the jet points most directly at us.

What's more, the EHT images show that the direction of the inner jet changes over time, providing clues as to what is driving the jet. From the images, the team also noticed features that appeared to move more slowly along a farther, particularly bright stretch of the jet. The bending towards Earth could explain both effects, as the flow can keep moving just as fast while looking brighter and shifting less laterally. Said MÃ¼ller:

We also found a clue about where the jet picks up speed. Even close to the apparent base of the jet, some features are already moving across the sky at apparent speeds comparable to those much farther downstream. If those features travel with the plasma, that suggests the jet gains much of its speed over a short distance near its base. As the fast flow narrows again, it may form a shock that adds to the brightness we see near the bend.

While 3C 279 is one of the best-studied quasars in radio astronomy, the mechanisms driving its central jet are still a mystery, and future observations could reveal behaviors that have not yet been seen. Astronomers have decades' worth of observations on how its jet behaves on larger scales, but only a few images on how it behaves at the sub-parsec level. Nevertheless, the EHT Collaboration is extremely useful because it enables deep surveys and high resolution, allowing astronomers to detect details in the jet's innermost region that weren't available before. Said MÃ¼ller:

This paper is just the beginning. We have EHT observations from several years, as well as observations at other frequencies that we scheduled around the same time, that are currently [being] analyzed. Observing at different frequencies lets us see different parts of the jet. Taking those observations close together helps us tell which differences come from the frequency we're using and which come from the jet itself changing.

We expect a series of results from these data over the next few years. Very few quasars have been studied in this much detail. That makes 3C 279 one of our best opportunities to understand how a black hole launches a jet and how that jet gets up to nearly the speed of light, and the current manuscript is just the beginning of that journey.

Further Reading: Astronomy & Astrophysics

We’re constantly testing and writing about pocket knives here at Popular Mechanics, and Benchmade is a brand that always tops our list of favorites. Its folders, automatics, flippers, and fixed blades are beautifully designed using all high-quality materials, and all are U.S.-made in its Oregon headquarters. But there’s no denying they’re pricey, costing upward of $200, and they rarely go on sale for much of a discount.

When the Osborne debuted in 2000, it was Benchmade’s first blade to sport the Axis lock, which been replicated in some form by nearly every major knife manufacturer since its patent expired in 2019. It’s designed for ambidextrous operation and fast, one-handed deployment, plus it keeps your fingers clear of the blade while you open and close the knife.

It has a longer drop-point tanto-style S90V stainless steel blade covered in the same stonewashed protective finish as the Bugout and Osborne, along with the same dark-green aluminum handle and copper accents. While it’s another great choice for EDC, the Bailout is outfitted with tactical-style elements, like the lanyard slot at the rear and the deep-carry clip.

#6381. Researchers Have Discovered a Previously Unknown Crystal Form of Silver

Researchers have discovered a previously unknown crystal structure of silver that exhibits unusually high chemical reactivity.

Silver can take on an extraordinarily rare atomic structure that makes it far more chemically reactive than its familiar form. Researchers at Hokkaido University have discovered a previously unknown crystal arrangement in which silver atoms form a simple cubic pattern, a structure previously documented in only one other element.

The findings, published in Nano Letters, emerged when scientists used an electron beam to break down silver iodide and observed the resulting silver crystals at the atomic scale. Unlike ordinary silver, the newly formed crystals began converting into silver oxide within approximately 100 seconds, demonstrating how dramatically atomic arrangement can influence a material’s chemical behavior.

Most silver crystallizes in a structure known as face-centered cubic, in which atoms occupy the eight corners and the center of each face of a repeating cube. This tightly packed arrangement is also found in common metals such as gold, copper, and aluminum.

The newly discovered silver instead formed a simple cubic structure, with atoms occupying only the corners of each repeating cube. This arrangement is exceptionally uncommon in pure elements. Before this discovery, the only known elemental example was radioactive polonium, whose simple cubic structure was identified in 1966.

“It was surprising to find that such a low-density structure could form in a pure metal crystal,” says first author Dr. Masaya Sakakibara. “We expected silver nanoparticles to form when silver iodide decomposes under electron beam irradiation, but we didn’t expect them to adopt a simple cubic structure.”

The researchers created and examined the silver using a transmission electron microscope (TEM), which employs electrons with wavelengths shorter than those of visible light to resolve structures down to individual atoms. The electron beam served two purposes: it triggered the decomposition of silver iodide and allowed the scientists to watch the resulting silver atoms organize into crystals.

The nanoscale conditions were essential to the discovery. At dimensions of just a few billionths of a meter, materials can temporarily adopt crystal structures that would be unstable in larger samples. Such arrangements can produce physical and chemical properties that differ substantially from those of the same element in its conventional form.

Experiments conducted under high vacuum revealed a striking difference between the two silver structures. Conventional face-centered cubic silver remained stable, while the simple cubic crystals gradually oxidized, forming silver oxide. The rapid transformation provided direct evidence of the new structure’s unusually high chemical reactivity.

“Within 100 seconds of its formation, it began to transform into silver oxide,” adds Sakakibara.

The researchers believe their technique could provide a way to discover other previously unknown crystal structures and investigate the properties they produce.

“This is a new approach to discovering previously unknown crystal structures, which could also help us develop materials with novel properties in the future,” says Professor Yuki Kimura, co-author of the study and head of the Low Temperature Nanomaterial Science Laboratory at Hokkaido University.

“Going forward, we will continue investigating the physical and chemical properties of simple cubic silver in greater detail and extend this approach to other elements and compounds.”

Reference: “Electron-Beam-Assisted Formation of Simple-Cubic Silver” by Masaya Sakakibara, Hiroki Nada, Yuji Kunisada, Tomoya Yamazaki and Yuki Kimura, 4 November 2026, Nano Letters. DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03635

#6380. Study Finds Artemis Astronauts Will Enjoy Moon-Grown Potatoes

By now, references to Mark Watney and how he grew potatoes in Martian soil have become a tired clichÃ©. Nevertheless, one can't help but recall the scene whenever news breaks about the latest experiment that examines the potential of growing plants in extraterrestrial soils. The latest comes from Oregon State University (OSU), where researchers have shown that potatoes grown in lunar soil simulant (amended with organic matter) are safe to eat and grow just as well as those produced on Earth.

This is good news for space agencies like NASA that are actively planning to send astronauts back to the Moon, and this time, to stay. Through the Artemis Program, crews will land around the South Pole-Aitken Basin and begin constructing a permanent base that will enable regular missions in the future (about one per year). China's National Space Agency (CNSA) and Roscosmos also plan on building a base - the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) - in the same region by the end of the decade.

To support long-term missions far from Earth, where opportunities for resupply will be fewer and farther between, a degree of self-sufficiency is required. Whereas the International Space Station (ISS) is resupplied regularly and emergency supplies can be dispatched within hours, missions to the Moon will take at least three days to arrive. As such, any sustained program of exploration on the Moon must rely on In-Situ Resource Utilization(ISRU) as much as possible - i.e., using local resources for building materials and providing astronauts with water and food.

Research in the past few decades has led to methods for 3D printing habitats and other facilities using lunar regolith. This can be combined with a bonding agent to create "lunacrete," or sintered with microwaves to create molten ceramic. Either material is then deposited layer by layer by construction robots to form walls and other structural elements. While hydroponics remain a viable way to grow plants (as astronauts do aboard the ISS), the real question is whether Earth plants can be grown in lunar regolith and other extraterrestrial soils.

Led by Aymeric Goyer, a professor with OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, the Oregon team used lunar regolith simulants with different levels of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich organic soil produced when earthworms break down organic matter. With support from NASA's Johnson Space Center Simulant Development Lab, the team produced healthy potatoes with yields comparable to crops grown by farmers in Oregon (the 4th largest potato producer in the U.S.).

Goyer and his teams specifically selected potatoes because they produce more calories per square meter of soil than many other crops. They also offer substantial nutritional value: one medium skin-on potato (148 g/5.3 oz) provides roughly 110 calories, 26 g of carbohydrates, 3 g of protein, and 2 g of fiber. They are also naturally fat-free, gluten-free, cholesterol-free, and are therefore considered a practical staple food for long-duration space missions.

Since lunar regolith varies across the Moon, the researchers tested five simulants representing lunar mare (fine-grained basaltic soil) and lunar highland (feldspar-rich volcanic soil) regions. They also included soil from Hermiston, Oregon, which produces the world's highest potato yield. The results showed that potato plants grown in simulants containing 30% vermicompost grew as well as those cultivated in Earth soils. In other samples, plants grown without vermicompost were severely stunted and had underdeveloped root systems.

The "Moon Village" concept, conceived by MIT in collaboration with the ESA and Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. Credit: ESA/Skidmore, Owings & Merrill

Lastly, those grown with 5% to 15% vermicompost showed only partial growth. As Goyer said in an OSU press release:

We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter. That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.

The results also showed that the potatoes grown in lunar regolith simulants maintained their nutritional quality, with no statistically significant increase in naturally occurring potato toxins (glycoalkaloids) often associated with green discoloration. Lunar regolith still presents many challenges for plant growth, which include extremely fine-grained dust and elevated levels of heavy metals.

But the researchers are confident that adding organic matter helps bind heavy metals, preventing them from damaging roots, interfering with growth, or leaching into the potatoes themselves. In the future, astronauts could bring compost to the Moon, along with Earth worms, to create their own fertilizer, augmenting soil collected during surface trips to grow their food.

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," said David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab. Their results are reported in a paper, "Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants," that appeared in npj Microgravity. Another paper, which reports the results of experiments involving 10 potato varieties to identify which grow best in lunar soil, will be released.

#6378. Scientists Discover the Human Ear May Work Very Differently Than We Thought

New research challenges a long-standing theory of how the inner ear detects sound, revealing a more complex process than previously understood.

Scientists have discovered that low-frequency sounds can produce nearly simultaneous vibrations across widely separated regions of the inner ear. The finding, observed in guinea pigs, challenges a long-standing model of how hearing works and could influence the development of more advanced cochlear implants.

For decades, scientists have understood the cochlea, the spiral-shaped structure inside the inner ear, as a frequency map. Different sounds activate different locations along its membrane, much like individual piano keys correspond to specific notes. High frequencies stimulate one end, while low frequencies primarily activate the other. This arrangement, known as the “place code,” has helped explain how the ear distinguishes sounds and forms a foundation of modern cochlear implant technology.

The traditional model dates back to research by Georg von Békésy, who received the 1961 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for demonstrating how different sound frequencies stimulate distinct regions of the cochlea. However, the new study, published in Science Advances, suggests that this location-based explanation does not fully account for how the inner ear processes low-frequency sounds.

To investigate, researchers used optical coherence tomography (OCT), an imaging technology (co-invented by OHSU physician-scientist David Huang) widely used in eye examinations. Combined with advanced signal processing to reduce background noise, the technique allowed scientists to detect extremely small vibrations at multiple locations inside the guinea pig cochlea.

The measurements showed that low-frequency sounds produced similar vibrations across distant regions, often with synchronized motion. Rather than disproving the cochlea’s frequency map, the findings indicate that additional mechanisms may contribute to how low-frequency information is represented and interpreted. The results build on earlier research published in 2022 that identified unexpected patterns of low-frequency responses.

Understanding low-frequency hearing is particularly important for interpreting complex sounds, including speech. These vibrations are difficult to measure experimentally, and people with hearing loss often struggle to understand conversations when background noise is present.

“When you bring in low-frequency background noise, it’s a very challenging environment for people with hearing loss,” said George Burwood, Ph.D., the study’s lead author and a research instructor at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU). “Also, the place code paradigm limits the interpretation of how mammals evolved to detect extremely complex signals, especially speech.”

Current cochlear implants use electrodes to electrically stimulate different regions of the cochlea according to sound frequency. The new findings suggest that reproducing more of the natural cochlea’s complex vibration patterns might improve how these devices convey sound information.

“Cochlear implants are geared to take advantage of a place code,” Burwood said. “Our study suggests the optimal pattern of stimulation by electrodes in a cochlear implant may be more complex than just where and how intensely it’s being stimulated.”

The findings also raise questions about how the auditory system separates frequencies when vibrations are distributed across multiple cochlear locations. Researchers suspect the brain may use information beyond the position of stimulation to distinguish certain sounds.

“This discovery advances our basic understanding in how hearing works,” said Larry Trussell, Ph.D., director of the Oregon Hearing Research Center at OHSU. “The brain appears to have mechanisms that are able to differentiate frequencies without having a map or place code.”

Reference: “Denoised vibrometry reveals noncanonical filtering at the apex of the cochlea” by George W. S. Burwood, Pierre Hakizimana, Karl Grosh, Wajiha Zaidi, Ruikang K. Wang, Alfred L. Nuttall and Anders Fridberger, 20 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aei4634

The research at OHSU was supported by the National Institutes of Health through award R01DC00141-44.

All research involving animal subjects at OHSU must be reviewed and approved by the university’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). The IACUC’s priority is to ensure the health and safety of animal research subjects. The IACUC also reviews procedures to ensure the health and safety of the people who work with the animals. No live animal work may be conducted at OHSU without IACUC approval.

#6377. Euclid's Record-Setting Quasar Probes Black Hole Formation

Quasars are the cosmos' most luminous objects, generated by supermassive black holes (SMBH) that are accreting enormous amounts of matter. Astronomers keep finding these massive objects further and further back in time. The ESA's Euclid just found the newest record holder: the telescope observed it 40 million years sooner than the previous record-holder, and it was found at redshift z=8.13, corresponding to about 630 million years after the Big Bang. That's firmly in the Epoch of Reionization.

The quasar's technical name is J1504+6252, but it's been given the more recognizable name DÃºn Aonghasa. DÃºn Aonghasa is an ancient stone fort on top of a cliff in Ireland, where it looks out over the Atlantic Ocean.

The discovery is in research published in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Euclid: Discovery of a quasar at z = 8.13 hosting a 360-million-solar-mass black hole." The lead author is Julien Wolf, who was a postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy when the research was done.

One of the hallmarks of modern astronomy is the discovery of massive objects in the Universe that formed much sooner than astronomers thought they could. The JWST is driving much of this.

"Quasars powered by rapid accretion onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) have been uncovered deep into the first gigayear of cosmic history," the authors write.

Now the Euclid Space Telescope is contributing to that trend. Euclid was launched to study dark energy and the expansion of the Universe. A big part of that job is measuring galaxies at different redshifts in its Euclid Wide Survey, to see how their morphologies are different over time. That will reveal how dark energy has changed over time.

This is what DÃºn Aonghasa, the new quasar, looks like in the actual Euclid image. It's the red dot in the center. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/J. Wolf et al.

Euclid found DÃºn Aonghasa in its Euclid Wide Survey imaging, but didn't confirm it. Follow-up observations by Keck, the Hubble, the Large Binocular Telescope, and especially the JWST provided the confirmation. JWST spectroscopy let the researchers measure "a systemic redshift of zsysâ=â8.129âÂ±â0.005, corresponding to only 630âMyr after the Big Bang and shifting the quasar redshift frontier by â39âMyr," the authors write. 39 million years is about 6% of the age of the Universe at that epoch. The quasar is now the first quasar observed at z > 8.

DÃºn Aonghasa's luminosity is what lets astronomers observe it at such a great distance. Its luminosity helped researchers measure its mass and its accretion rate, and DÃºn Aonghasa contains 360 million solar masses.

This figure shows absolute UV magnitude as a function of redshift for high-redshift quasars, galaxies, LRDs, LBDs, and other JWST-selected AGN up to zâ=â11. Orange squares show recently identified Euclid quasars, and the green star shows DÃºn Aonghasa, which is more UV-luminous than the LRDs, other JWST-selected AGN, and Lyman-break galaxies at comparable redshifts. JWST-selected AGN are shown as circles and colour-coded according to their phenomenological classification: LRDs in red, LBDs in blue, and other AGN in black. Previously known quasars are shown as grey circles. Open purple diamonds are Lyman-break galaxies. Image Credit: J. Wolf et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A356

DÃºn Aonghasa and its high redshift brethren pose the same familiar question: how did they get so large so quickly?

"Assembling a black hole of several hundred million solar masses within the first few hundred million years, despite its currently sub-Eddington accretion rate, requires either a massive seed or sustained, highly efficient early growth," the authors write.

While an actual answer to their growth is elusive, finding them helps constrain an eventual answer.

âFinding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew,â said lead author Wolf in a press release. âThe closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth â or both.â

Aside from their puzzling masses, these quasars also open different windows or probes into aspects of the early Universe. They give astronomers long sightlines into the intergalactic medium, letting them study its opacity during reionization, and its metal enrichment.

The quasars also serve as probes of how matter was distributed. "Quasars further mark rare, highly biased peaks in the underlying matter distribution and therefore trace the densest regions of the early large-scale structure," the researchers write.

On galactic scales, these high-redshift quasars are probes of how SMBH masses and the masses of their host galaxies co-evolved. Both masses tend to correlate, but there's no obvious reason why. AGN feedback could play a role, so could mergers, or a shared source of fuel for growth. But there's no certainty, so finding more high-redshift quasars may lead to an answer.

These things are all related, but the main result of finding these quasars is facing the questions posed by their high masses.

Finding these quasars and supermassive black holes is forcing astronomers to consider different explanations for how they grew so massive so quickly. One explanation is super-Eddington accretion, but DÃºn Aonghasa isn't accreting matter that rapidly. Another is massive seeds, but current formation models struggle to accommodate those. Another explanation is that quasars experienced super-Eddington accretion very early in the Universe, under very different conditions.

Heavy seeds could explain these quasars, but what could they be? Astrophysicists don't know, but some candidates are Direct-Collapse Black Holes, or maybe sequential runaway stellar collisions in extremely dense star clusters.

Another, more exotic and theoretical possibility for heavy seeds is primordial black holes (PBH). These are theorized to have formed in the very first moments in the Universe, when dense pockets of gas collapsed directly into black holes. With such an early head start, these PBH could've formed into heavy seeds without needing physics-breaking levels of accretion.

Primordial black holes are only hypothetical. If they're real, they could've formed by direct collapse of dense pockets of matter shortly after the Big Bang. They could've acted as seeds for the very early, very massive SMBH found in the Epoch of Reionization. Image Credit: ESA/Hubble, N. Bartmann., CC BY-SA

Luminous quasars like DÃºn Aonghasa are rare in the Epoch of Reionization. So far, there are only seven of them. The only path to an explanation for their masses is through more observations that find more of these ancient quasars, and hopefully ones even more distant.

âAnd this may happen sooner than we think,â said co-author Silvia Belladitta a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy. âThis highlights how quickly Euclid is expanding our census of the most distant quasars. Each new discovery brings us closer to understanding how supermassive black holes formed and grew in the early universe.â

"DÃºn Aonghasa establishes a new quasar redshift frontier as the first confirmed quasar at zâ>â8, providing a powerful new benchmark for early SMBH growth," the researchers write in their paper's conclusion. Its large mass shows that it must have grown a lot before it was observed, but its bolometric luminosity contradicts that. So the mystery of massive early SMBH and their quasars is still a puzzle.

Researchers predicted that Euclid will find between 8â23 quasars at zâ>â8, so hopefully, more are on their way.

âIt is unclear how far back in time these supermassive black holes powering luminous quasars exist, but Euclid has a good chance of finding out what that limit is,â said MPIA scientist and co-author Eduardo BaÃ±ados.

It might seem like researchers are chasing a receding horizon, almost like a dog chasing its tail. They build better telescopes in hopes of finding answers to difficult questions. Then their telescopes uncover some answers, but also uncover more questions. It's probably true that there's no end to knowledge and we'll never know everything. But that also means there's no end to learning, no end to Nature, and no end to wonder.

#6375. How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

North Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for new member orientation. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

But as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” said Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

“Nobody could have predicted this,’’ said David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

But the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

“In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown said, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

“Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”

Womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic issues. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

“There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she said in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”

Womack said her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” said Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis said. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

“I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he said in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a new map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

“North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he said. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he said.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”

#6373. Scientists Discover an Ancient Herbal Remedy May Help Curb Binge Drinking

A supplement derived from kudzu, a plant used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, may help people with alcohol use disorder reduce binge drinking without taking medication every day.

In a clinical trial led by researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF), people who took a standardized kudzu extract before anticipated episodes of heavy drinking experienced significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those given a placebo. The benefits persisted for three months after participants stopped taking the supplement.

The findings, published in the American Journal of Psychiatry on November 4, suggest that taking a treatment during periods of heightened risk could offer a new strategy for managing problematic alcohol consumption.

Binge drinking accounts for more than half of the roughly 80,000 annual U.S. deaths attributed to excessive alcohol consumption. Despite the scale of the problem, fewer than 10% of people with alcohol use disorder have ever received medication to treat the condition.

“Binge drinking is incredibly common, but we don’t have many tools to offer people who want to cut back,” said Glenn-Milo Santos, PhD, MPH, the study’s lead author and a UCSF professor of community health systems. “Our goal is to expand that toolkit. What’s exciting about this approach is that people can use it when they know they may be at risk of heavy drinking, rather than taking a medication every day.”

The trial involved 120 adults with alcohol use disorder who engaged in binge drinking at least once a week. Binge drinking was defined as consuming at least five alcoholic drinks on a single occasion for men and at least four for women.

Participants were divided into two groups, with half receiving a standardized kudzu extract and the other half receiving a placebo. Over 12 weeks, they were instructed to take their assigned treatment approximately 2.5 hours before they anticipated drinking heavily. Everyone also received brief weekly counseling sessions.

By the end of the trial, participants taking kudzu had reduced their average number of binge-drinking days from 2.15 to 1.42 per week. Those receiving the placebo showed little improvement, with their weekly average declining from 2.15 to 2.06 days.

Kudzu also reduced how frequently participants experienced weeks involving any binge drinking. The proportion of such weeks dropped from 88% to 58% among those taking the extract, compared with a decline from 88% to 81% in the placebo group.

Three months after the treatment period ended, participants who had received kudzu continued to report significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those in the placebo group. Researchers suggest that drinking less during the trial may have helped participants reconsider their drinking habits and develop greater confidence in their ability to control their alcohol consumption.

Participants tolerated the kudzu extract well, experiencing no more side effects than those receiving the placebo. No serious adverse effects were linked to the treatment.

However, the researchers caution against assuming that commercially available kudzu supplements will deliver comparable benefits. The trial used a standardized formulation, whereas the composition of products sold over the counter can vary considerably. Larger clinical studies are needed to confirm the results across more diverse populations.

Reference: “Targeted Use of Kudzu for Binge Drinking Among Adults With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Phase 2b Randomized Trial” by Glenn-Milo Santos, Phillip Coffin, Allie Dunham, Thomas Hoffmann, John Walker, Tim Matheson and Steven Batki, 3 November 2026, American Journal of Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1176/appi.ajp.20251354

This study was funded by National Institutes for Health (R01AA025930). Santos is also supported by a K24 career development grant from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), which is part of the NIH.

#6372. A Newly Discovered Group of Immune Cells May Be Working Against You

Researchers have identified a previously unknown group of aging immune cells that may undermine the body’s natural defenses.

Some aging immune cells do more than lose their ability to fight disease. Researchers at Monash University have identified a previously unknown group of immune cells that actively suppress the body’s defenses, potentially helping explain why cancer and serious infections become more common with age.

The discovery comes from a preclinical study published in Science Immunology. Using mouse models, scientists mapped genetic changes that cause immune cells to deteriorate in different ways, identifying potential targets for treatments aimed at preserving immune function later in life.

The researchers investigated CD8+ T cells, immune cells responsible for recognizing and destroying infected and cancerous cells. They identified three distinct ways aging disrupts the genetic programs controlling these cells, impairing their ability to respond to unfamiliar threats, regulate immune activity, and maintain normal cellular health.

“Aging is the biggest risk factor for cancer overall,” said Dr. Daniel Thiele, the study’s first author at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute. “Our immune system is constantly surveying our bodies for potentially cancerous cells and eliminating them, often without us ever knowing.”

“As we age, this natural defense system becomes less effective, making us more vulnerable to cancer and infections and reducing our ability to respond to vaccines.”

“This study provides a blueprint of immune aging, from which we can now identify potential targets to reverse aspects of that decline.”

The findings challenge the idea that immune cells simply become progressively weaker as they age. Some lose their protective functions, while others develop the ability to interfere with neighboring immune cells. These different patterns can occur within the same aging individual.

“Even within the same aging individual, we found that immune cells can age in remarkably different ways,” Dr. Thiele said. “Some cells lose their ability to protect us against disease, while others begin to interfere with the body’s own immune defenses.”

“By understanding what goes wrong within these cells, we can begin to identify more targeted ways to restore immune function as we age.”

The research has also contributed to a separate discovery involving granzyme K, a protein produced by immune cells. In that study, Monash scientists identified granzyme K as a driver of age-related organ damage in mice, suggesting that changes in immune cell behavior may affect tissues beyond the immune system itself.

The findings raise the possibility of developing therapies that address specific mechanisms of immune aging rather than attempting to stimulate the entire immune system. Such treatments remain a future prospect, with the current evidence coming from preclinical research.

“By understanding what drives aging within our immune cells, we may ultimately be able to target not only immune aging, but aging throughout the body,” said Professor Nicole La Gruta, the study’s senior researcher at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute.

Reference: “Aging drives distinct chromatin signatures of CD8 T cell dysfunction and the emergence of a unique CD8 Treg cell population” by Daniel Thiele, Liam C. Kealy, David Chisanga, Brendan E. Russ, Angela Nguyen, Jessica Runting, Iona S. Schuster, Adele Barugahare, Tabinda Hussain, Mohammad Asadian, Minh Bui, Taylah J. Bennett, Nemo Shindo, Justin B. Zhang, Jasmine Li, Mariapia A. Degli-Esposti, Axel Kallies, Kim Good-Jacobson, Colby Zaph, Stephen J. Turner and Nicole L. La Gruta, 20 November 2026, Science Immunology. DOI: 10.1126/sciimmunol.aej5412

The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition.

These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found.

Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes, which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure.

One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on.

"These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain."

In the new study, published Friday (Nov. 20) in the journal Cell Reports, scientists took a close look at DNA methylation in 302 brains that had been donated after death. These included 101 brains from individuals diagnosed with PTSD, 101 from people with major depressive disorder and 100 from people without any diagnosed psychiatric disorders. The researchers also had access to these individuals' medical records.

The team zoomed in on three brain regions: the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala and the hippocampus. The prefrontal cortex handles cognitive functions like planning and decision-making, the amygdala is a major hub for emotional processing, and the hippocampus is key for memory and learning.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"The goal of our study was to look at the epigenetics of the PTSD brain and ask how [it] is different from that of an individual who does not have PTSD," Champagne said, "or who comparatively has another diagnosis, like major depressive disorder."

Compared to the brains of people without any disorders, the brains of people with PTSD had different patterns of methylation in the prefrontal cortex, in particular. By contrast, in major depressive disorder, the amygdala stood out as a brain region with distinct methylation.

Additionally, in depression, the observed differences in methylation tended to affect the same set of genes across different regions of the brain. This was not the case in PTSD, which showed more inconsistencies in terms of which specific genes were involved. The methylation patterns in PTSD also appeared to vary depending on other factors, such as patients' sex, ethnicity and age at which they experienced trauma.

The study's results serve as a valuable resource, said Seyma Katrinli, an investigator in the Grady Trauma Project, a large PTSD study, at the Emory University School of Medicine.

Although the findings can't be used to help diagnose PTSD yet, down the line, this area of research could help scientists correlate changes that are measurable in people's blood to changes in the brain, said Katrinli, who was not involved in the new work. Then, blood tests could help guide the diagnosis and treatment of PTSD, she suggested.

That said, the study had limitations. Because the scientists analyzed postmortem brains, they relied on the medical reports rather than assessing the study subjects directly. Additionally, both PTSD and major depressive disorder are associated with substance use, which also causes DNA methylation; this potential confounding factor was not accounted for in the study. .

Finally, at this point, there is no way to tell what triggered the observed differences in DNA methylation. The scientists can't say if the variations are a consequence of PTSD, a risk factor for PTSD, or a downstream effect of other things that co-occur with PTSD.

The research sets the stage to "help us ask better questions," Champagne said. Her team is now looking to investigate factors — such as sex, the timing of traumatic experiences, or history of substance use — that may be driving the variation within PTSD.

"It's a very exciting foray into epigenetic profiling in the brain," she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Wylie, D., Arasappan, D., Ross, D., Hyde, T. M., Ressler, K. J., Kleinman, J. E., Weinberger, D. R., Daskalakis, N. P., Nemeroff, C. B., & Champagne, F. A. (2026). DNA methylation profiling of human brain in posttraumatic stress and major depressive disorders indicate specific molecular features. Cell Reports, 118270. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118270

#6368. “This Star System Should Not Exist”: Astronomers Discover a Cosmic Mystery Just 28 Light-Years Away

A red dwarf still circles the burned-out core of a star that could once have swallowed it, and their orbit is wider than astronomers expected.

A planet too faint to see can still give itself away by making the star it orbits wobble. Astronomers looking for planets around a dim red star 28 light-years from Earth measured a wobble more than a thousand times larger than they expected. Following that motion revealed a family of three stars, two of which had already run out of fuel.

“We were actually looking for planets,” said lead author Étienne Artigau, a researcher at Université de Montréal’s Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx). “Instead, we found something much more surprising.”

The star they were watching was a red dwarf, a star much dimmer than the Sun. At the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi, a planet-hunting instrument called SPIRou (SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge) picked up a change of nearly 16 kilometers (10 miles) per second in the star’s speed. After several years of follow-up observations, the team knew that whatever was tugging on the red dwarf had more than half the Sun’s mass.

“The unusual combination of high mass and very low brightness left only one plausible explanation: it was the remnant of a dead star,” said Charles-Antoine Parent, an undergraduate student at Université Laval and co-author of the study. “The most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldn’t be ruled out.”

The team finally saw the faint companion with Gemini North, another telescope on Maunakea. High-resolution images from its ʻAlopeke instrument showed a white dwarf orbiting the red dwarf. A white dwarf is the extremely dense core a star leaves behind after it runs out of fuel. Most stars, including the Sun, will end their lives this way.

Astronomers already knew about a white dwarf much farther out. That outer star circles both the red dwarf and its newly spotted companion. No other trio like this one, named Welopōʻai, is known within 100 light-years of Earth.

Before it became a white dwarf, the red dwarf’s closer neighbor was about 40 percent more massive than the Sun. As it aged, it swelled into a giant several hundred times its original size. The red dwarf would have been close enough for the expanding giant to affect it. In similar systems, a giant can swallow its companion, and the two stars can even merge. Welopōʻai’s red dwarf appears to have survived. It now circles the remnant in a stable orbit, farther away than astronomers would expect given how close the two once were.

“This system should not exist,” said Patrick Dufour, a professor at Université de Montréal who studies white dwarfs and co-authored the paper. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.”

The team wants to find out whether the pull of all three stars on one another could explain the inner pair’s orbit. The researchers also measured the inner white dwarf’s mass with an uncertainty of less than 1 percent. Astronomers rarely get such a precise mass for a white dwarf, and it gives them a way to test predictions about how stars age and how matter behaves when packed so tightly together. The international team, led by IREx, reported its in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

The simulation illustrates how gravitational interactions between its three stars could influence their orbits over time. The sonification translates the stars’ orbital motions into sound, so you can hear the system’s changing rhythms. Credit: Heidi White (UMONTREAL/IREx). Simulation data: Alexandre Correia, University of Coimbra

Welopōʻai got its name through A Hua He Inoa (“To Call Forth a Name”), a program of the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi. The name joins welo, an inherited or family trait, with pōʻai, an orbit or circular path. Together they evoke a “path of family traits.”

“Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,” Artigau said. “Even when we’re searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us.”

Reference: “Welopō‘ai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun” by Étienne Artigau, Charles-Antoine Parent, Atanas K. Stefanov, Érika Le Bourdais, Souleymane Ouedraogo, Alexandrine L’Heureux, Patrick Dufour, René Doyon, Neil J. Cook, Charles Cadieux, Clémence Fontanive, Luc Arnold, Jean-François Donati, Matthias R. Schreiber, Ryan Cloutier, Xavier Delfosse, Céline Reylé, Thierry Forveille, Tianqi Cang, Claire Moutou and Alexandre C. M. Correia, 19 November 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics. DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202661214
